# simplelog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/simplelog/

## Expand description

`simplelog` provides a series of logging facilities, that can be easily combined.

- `SimpleLogger`(very basic logger that logs to stdout)
- `TermLogger`(advanced terminal logger, that splits to stdout/err and has color support) (can be excluded on unsupported platforms)
- `WriteLogger`(logs to a given struct implementing- `Write`, e.g. a file)
- `CombinedLogger`(can be used to form combinations of the above loggers)
- `TestLogger`(specialized logger for tests. Uses print!() / println!() for tests to be able to capture the output)

Only one Logger should be initialized of the start of your program
through the `Logger::init(...)` method. For the actual calling syntax
take a look at the documentation of the specific implementation(s) you wanna use.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Combined](https://docs.rs/struct.CombinedLogger.html)- Logger
- The CombinedLogger struct. Provides a Logger implementation that proxies multiple Loggers as one.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- Configuration for the Loggers
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for the Logger Configurations (`Config`)
- [Simple](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleLogger.html)- Logger
- The SimpleLogger struct. Provides a very basic Logger implementation
- [Term](https://docs.rs/struct.TermLogger.html)- Logger
- The TermLogger struct. Provides a stderr/out based Logger implementation
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteLogger.html)- Logger
- The WriteLogger struct. Provides a Logger implementation for structs implementing `Write`, e.g. File

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)
- The set of available colors for the terminal foreground/background.
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- ColorChoice represents the color preferences of an end user.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.FormatItem.html)- Item
- A complete description of how to format and parse a type.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)
- An enum representing the available verbosity levels of the logger.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)- Filter
- An enum representing the available verbosity level filters of the logger.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the level
- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.TargetPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the thread id/name
- [Terminal](https://docs.rs/enum.TerminalMode.html)- Mode
- Specifies which streams should be used when logging
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/enum.ThreadLogMode.html)- LogMode
- Mode for logging the thread name or id or both.
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/enum.ThreadPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the thread id/name

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Shared](https://docs.rs/trait.SharedLogger.html)- Logger
- Trait to have a common interface to obtain the Level of Loggers

# simplelog 0.12.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/simplelog/latest

## A simple and easy-to-use logging facility for Rust's [log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate

`simplelog` does not aim to provide a rich set of features, nor to provide the
best logging solution. It aims to be a maintainable, easy to integrate facility
for small to medium sized projects, that find [env_logger](https://crates.io/crates/env_logger)
to be somewhat lacking in features. In those cases `simplelog` should provide an
easy alternative.

## Concept

`simplelog` provides a series of logging facilities, that can be easily combined.

- `SimpleLogger`(very basic logger that logs to stderr/out, should never fail)
- `TermLogger`(advanced terminal logger, that splits to stderr/out and has color support) (can be excluded on unsupported platforms)
- `WriteLogger`(logs to a given struct implementing- `Write`. e.g. a file)
- `CombinedLogger`(can be used to form combinations of the above loggers)

## Usage

```
 extern crate log;
extern crate simplelog;
use *;
use File;
```
### Results in

```
$ cargo run --example usage
   Compiling simplelog v0.12.2 (file:///home/drakulix/Projects/simplelog)
     Running `target/debug/examples/usage`
[ERROR] Bright red error
```
and my_rust_binary.log

```
11:13:03 [ERROR] usage: Bright red error
11:13:03 [INFO] usage: This only appears in the log file
```
## Getting Started

Just add

```
[dependencies]
simplelog = "^0.12.2"
```
to your `Cargo.toml`

## ANSI color and style support

This crate can internally depend on a [paris](https://github.com/0x20F/paris) crate to provide support for ANSI color and styles.
To use this feature you need to set a *paris* feature, like this:

```
[dependencies]
simplelog = { version = "^0.12.2", features = ["paris"] }
```
in your `Cargo.toml`

After this you can use e.g. the following call:

```
info!;
```
This will automatically generates terminal control sequences for desired styles.

More formatting info: [paris crate documentation](https://github.com/0x20F/paris)

## Contributing

If you wish to contribute your own logger to `simplelog` or advance/extend existing loggers,
feel free to create a pull request. Just don't blindly assume, that your logger will be accepted.
The rational about this library is, that it is simple to use. This mostly comes down to a small
and easy API, but also includes things like the amount of added dependencies. If you feel unsure
about your plans, feel free to create an issue to talk about your ideas.

---

# ansi_term - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ansi_term/^0.12/

## Expand description

This is a library for controlling colours and formatting, such as red bold text or blue underlined text, on ANSI terminals.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage)Basic usage

There are three main types in this crate that you need to be
concerned with: [ ANSIString](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIString.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[.](https://docs.rs/enum.Colour.html)

`Colour`A `Style` holds stylistic information: foreground and background colours,
whether the text should be bold, or blinking, or other properties. The
[ Colour](https://docs.rs/enum.Colour.html) enum represents the available colours. And an

[is a string paired with a](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIString.html)

`ANSIString`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[ Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html) is also available as an alias to

`Colour`.To format a string, call the `paint` method on a `Style` or a `Colour`,
passing in the string you want to format as the argument. For example,
here’s how to get some red text:

```
use ansi_term::Colour::Red;
println!("This is in red: {}", Red.paint("a red string"));
```
It’s important to note that the `paint` method does *not* actually return a
string with the ANSI control characters surrounding it. Instead, it returns
an [ ANSIString](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIString.html) value that has a

[implementation that, when formatted, returns the characters. This allows strings to be printed with a minimum of](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display`[allocations being performed behind the scenes.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html)

`String`If you *do* want to get at the escape codes, then you can convert the
[ ANSIString](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIString.html) to a string as you would any other

`Display` value:```
use ansi_term::Colour::Red;
let red_string = Red.paint("a red string").to_string();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#bold-underline-background-and-other-styles)Bold, underline, background, and other styles

For anything more complex than plain foreground colour changes, you need to
construct `Style` values themselves, rather than beginning with a `Colour`.
You can do this by chaining methods based on a new `Style`, created with
[ Style::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.new). Each method creates a new style that has that specific
property set. For example:

```
use ansi_term::Style;
println!("How about some {} and {}?",
         Style::new().bold().paint("bold"),
         Style::new().underline().paint("underline"));
```
For brevity, these methods have also been implemented for `Colour` values,
so you can give your styles a foreground colour without having to begin with
an empty `Style` value:

```
use ansi_term::Colour::{Blue, Yellow};
println!("Demonstrating {} and {}!",
         Blue.bold().paint("blue bold"),
         Yellow.underline().paint("yellow underline"));
println!("Yellow on blue: {}", Yellow.on(Blue).paint("wow!"));
```
The complete list of styles you can use are: [ bold](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.bold),

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.dimmed)

`dimmed`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.italic)

`italic`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.underline)

`underline`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.blink)

`blink`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.reverse)

`reverse`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.hidden)

`hidden`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.strikethrough)

`strikethrough`[for background colours.](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.on)

`on`In some cases, you may find it easier to change the foreground on an
existing `Style` rather than starting from the appropriate `Colour`.
You can do this using the [ fg](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.fg) method:

```
use ansi_term::Style;
use ansi_term::Colour::{Blue, Cyan, Yellow};
println!("Yellow on blue: {}", Style::new().on(Blue).fg(Yellow).paint("yow!"));
println!("Also yellow on blue: {}", Cyan.on(Blue).fg(Yellow).paint("zow!"));
```
You can turn a `Colour` into a `Style` with the [ normal](https://docs.rs/enum.Colour.html#method.normal) method.
This will produce the exact same

`ANSIString` as if you just used the
`paint` method on the `Colour` directly, but it’s useful in certain cases:
for example, you may have a method that returns `Styles`, and need to
represent both the “red bold” and “red, but not bold” styles with values of
the same type. The `Style` struct also has a [implementation if you want to have a style with](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`*nothing*set.

```
use ansi_term::Style;
use ansi_term::Colour::Red;
Red.normal().paint("yet another red string");
Style::default().paint("a completely regular string");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#extended-colours)Extended colours

You can access the extended range of 256 colours by using the `Colour::Fixed`
variant, which takes an argument of the colour number to use. This can be
included wherever you would use a `Colour`:

```
use ansi_term::Colour::Fixed;
Fixed(134).paint("A sort of light purple");
Fixed(221).on(Fixed(124)).paint("Mustard in the ketchup");
```
The first sixteen of these values are the same as the normal and bold
standard colour variants. There’s nothing stopping you from using these as
`Fixed` colours instead, but there’s nothing to be gained by doing so
either.

You can also access full 24-bit colour by using the `Colour::RGB` variant,
which takes separate `u8` arguments for red, green, and blue:

```
use ansi_term::Colour::RGB;
RGB(70, 130, 180).paint("Steel blue");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#combining-successive-coloured-strings)Combining successive coloured strings

The benefit of writing ANSI escape codes to the terminal is that they
*stack*: you do not need to end every coloured string with a reset code if
the text that follows it is of a similar style. For example, if you want to
have some blue text followed by some blue bold text, it’s possible to send
the ANSI code for blue, followed by the ANSI code for bold, and finishing
with a reset code without having to have an extra one between the two
strings.

This crate can optimise the ANSI codes that get printed in situations like
this, making life easier for your terminal renderer. The [ ANSIStrings](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIStrings.html)
type takes a slice of several

[values, and will iterate over each of them, printing only the codes for the styles that need to be updated as part of its formatting routine.](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIString.html)

`ANSIString`The following code snippet uses this to enclose a binary number displayed in red bold text inside some red, but not bold, brackets:

```
use ansi_term::Colour::Red;
use ansi_term::{ANSIString, ANSIStrings};
let some_value = format!("{:b}", 42);
let strings: &[ANSIString<'static>] = &[
    Red.paint("["),
    Red.bold().paint(some_value),
    Red.paint("]"),
];
println!("Value: {}", ANSIStrings(strings));
```
There are several things to note here. Firstly, the [ paint](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIByteString.html#method.write_to) method can take

*either*an owned

[or a borrowed](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/string/struct.String.html)

`String`[. Internally, an](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[holds a copy-on-write (](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIString.html)

`ANSIString`[) string value to deal with both owned and borrowed strings at the same time. This is used here to display a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/borrow/enum.Cow.html)

`Cow``String`,
the result of the `format!` call, using the same mechanism as some
statically-available `&str` slices. Secondly, that the [value works in the same way as its singular counterpart, with a](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIStrings.html)

`ANSIStrings`[implementation that only performs the formatting when required.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display`[§](https://docs.rs#byte-strings)Byte strings

This library also supports formatting `\[u8]` byte strings; this supports
applications working with text in an unknown encoding.  [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html) and

[support painting](https://docs.rs/enum.Colour.html)

`Colour``\[u8]` values, resulting in an [. This type does not implement](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIByteString.html)

`ANSIByteString`[, as it may not contain UTF-8, but it does provide a method](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Display.html)

`Display`[to write the result to any value that implements](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIByteString.html#method.write_to)

`write_to`[:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`Write````
use ansi_term::Colour::Green;
Green.paint("user data".as_bytes()).write_to(&mut std::io::stdout()).unwrap();
```
Similarly, the type [ ANSIByteStrings](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIByteStrings.html) supports writing a list of

[values with minimal escape sequences:](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIByteString.html)

`ANSIByteString````
use ansi_term::Colour::Green;
use ansi_term::ANSIByteStrings;
ANSIByteStrings(&[
    Green.paint("user data 1\n".as_bytes()),
    Green.bold().paint("user data 2\n".as_bytes()),
]).write_to(&mut std::io::stdout()).unwrap();
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [Colour](https://docs.rs/enum.Colour.html)as Color;

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/struct.ANSIGenericString.html)- Generic - String
- An `ANSIGenericString`includes a generic string type and a`Style`to display that string.`ANSIString`and`ANSIByteString`are aliases for this type on`str`and`\[u8]`, respectively.
- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/struct.ANSIGenericStrings.html)- Generic - Strings
- A set of `ANSIGenericString`s collected together, in order to be written with a minimum of control characters.
- [Infix](https://docs.rs/struct.Infix.html)
- Like `ANSIString`, but only displays the difference between two styles.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/struct.Prefix.html)
- Like `ANSIString`, but only displays the style prefix.
- [Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)
- A style is a collection of properties that can format a string using ANSI escape codes.
- [Suffix](https://docs.rs/struct.Suffix.html)
- Like `ANSIString`, but only displays the style suffix.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Colour](https://docs.rs/enum.Colour.html)
- A colour is one specific type of ANSI escape code, and can refer to either the foreground or background colour.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/fn.ANSIByteStrings.html)- Byte - Strings
- A function to construct an `ANSIByteStrings`instance.
- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/fn.ANSIStrings.html)- Strings
- A function to construct an `ANSIStrings`instance.
- [sub_](https://docs.rs/fn.sub_string.html)- string
- Return a substring of the given ANSIStrings sequence, while keeping the formatting.
- [unstyle](https://docs.rs/fn.unstyle.html)
- Return a concatenated copy of `strs`without the formatting, as an allocated`String`.
- [unstyled_](https://docs.rs/fn.unstyled_len.html)- len
- Return the unstyled length of ANSIStrings. This is equaivalent to `unstyle(strs).len()`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIByteString.html)- Byte - String
- An `ANSIByteString`represents a formatted series of bytes. Use`ANSIByteString`when styling text with an unknown encoding.
- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIByteStrings.html)- Byte - Strings
- A set of `ANSIByteString`s collected together, in order to be written with a minimum of control characters.
- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIString.html)- String
- An ANSI String is a string coupled with the `Style`to display it in a terminal.
- [ANSI](https://docs.rs/type.ANSIStrings.html)- Strings
- A set of `ANSIString`s collected together, in order to be written with a minimum of control characters.

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/0.4.*/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# paris - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/paris/~1.5/

## Expand description

Simple way to output beautiful text in your CLI applications. Only limit is your imagination.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use)How to use

```
use paris::Logger;
let mut log = Logger::new();
log.info("It's that simple!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#simple-api)Simple api

```
// You can have icons at the start of your message!
log.info("Will add ℹ at the start");
log.error("Will add ✖ at the start");
 // or as macros
info!("Will add ℹ at the start");
error!("Will add ✖ at the start");
```
See [the Logger struct](https://docs.rs/paris/) for all methods

[§](https://docs.rs#chaining)Chaining

All methods can be chained together to build more intricate log/message combinations, in hopes of minimizing the chaos that every log string becomes when you have to concatenate a bunch of strings and add tabs and newlines everywhere.

```
log.info("this is some info")
   .indent(4).warn("this is now indented by 4")
   .newline(5)
   .success("and this is 5 lines under all other messages");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#customisation)Customisation

Outputting text is cool. Outputting text with a colored icon at the start is even cooler! But this crate is all about customisation, about making the logs feel like home, if you will. Included in the crate are a variety of keys you can use to colorize your logs just the way you want them to be.

```
log.info("I can write normal text or use tags to <red>color it</>");
log.warn("Every function can contain <on-green><black>tags</>");
log.info("If you don't write them <what>correctly</>, you just get an ugly looking tag");
```
There’s a key for all colors supported by the terminal `(white, black, red, blue, magenta, etc.)`
If you add the word `on` to any of those colors, it becomes the
background color instead `(on red, on blue, on green)`.

```
// How useful...
log.info("<on-red> This has red background </>");
```
Maybe you’d like to use your terminals brighter colors, if that’s the case
you just have to add `bright` to your tag. Makes sense.

`log.info("<blue><on-bright-red> This text is blue on a bright red background</> it's a pain");`If you feel like writing a lot of colors by hand is too tedious, or if you know you’re going
to be using the same combination of colors over and over again you can create a `custom style`
that encapsulates all those colors.

```
log.add_style("lol", vec!["green", "bold", "on-bright-blue"]);
// '<lol>' is now a key that you can use in your strings
log.info("<lol>This is has all your new styles</>");
```
See [the README](https://github.com/SirTheViking/logger/blob/master/README.md) for a full list of keys
if you’re not feeling confident in your ability to name colors. It happens.

[§](https://docs.rs#resetting)Resetting

You’ve probably seen the `</>` tag in the above logs. It’s not there to
*“close the previously opened tag”* no no. You can open as many tags as you want
and only use `</>` once, it’s just the *“reset everything to default”* tag, You might
decide you don’t ever want to use it. It’s up to you.
However, resetting everything to default might not be what you want. Most of the time
it’ll be enough, but for those times when it isn’t there are a few other tags such as:

- `<///>`only resets the background
- `<//>`only reset the foreground

[§](https://docs.rs#macros)Macros

With the macros feature enabled, you get access to macro equivalents of the logger functions.

Advantages of using macros:

- You don’t have to instantiate the logger `Logger::new()`
- Simple to write
- Can format parameters like `print!`and`println!`

Disadvantages of using macros:

- Can’t chain calls
- Manual newlines and tabs with `\n`and`\t`
- There’s no loading animation for macros

You get to decide whether you want to use macros or not.
Every macro has the same functionality as its `Logger`
equivalent. Colors and icon keys work just the same.

See [the Logger struct](https://docs.rs/paris/) for all methods and their macro equivalents

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use formatter::`- [LogIcon](https://docs.rs/formatter/enum.LogIcon.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [formatter](https://docs.rs/formatter/index.html)
- A wrapper around a few functions to make finding and replacing keys inside a string easier.
- [output](https://docs.rs/output/index.html)
- Helper functions for writing to stdout/stderr

---

# termcolor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/termcolor/^1.1/

## Expand description

This crate provides a cross platform abstraction for writing colored text to a terminal. Colors are written using either ANSI escape sequences or by communicating with a Windows console. Much of this API was motivated by use inside command line applications, where colors or styles can be configured by the end user and/or the environment.

This crate also provides platform independent support for writing colored text to an in memory buffer. While this is easy to do with ANSI escape sequences (because they are in the buffer themselves), it is trickier to do with the Windows console API, which requires synchronous communication.

In ANSI mode, this crate also provides support for writing hyperlinks.

[§](https://docs.rs#organization)Organization

The `WriteColor` trait extends the `io::Write` trait with methods for setting
colors or resetting them.

`StandardStream` and `StandardStreamLock` both satisfy `WriteColor` and are
analogous to `std::io::Stdout` and `std::io::StdoutLock`, or `std::io::Stderr`
and `std::io::StderrLock`.

`Buffer` is an in memory buffer that supports colored text. In a parallel
program, each thread might write to its own buffer. A buffer can be printed to
using a `BufferWriter`. The advantage of this design is that each thread can
work in parallel on a buffer without having to synchronize access to global
resources such as the Windows console. Moreover, this design also prevents
interleaving of buffer output.

`Ansi` and `NoColor` both satisfy `WriteColor` for arbitrary implementors of
`io::Write`. These types are useful when you know exactly what you need. An
analogous type for the Windows console is not provided since it cannot exist.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-using-standardstream)Example: using `StandardStream`

The `StandardStream` type in this crate works similarly to `std::io::Stdout`,
except it is augmented with methods for coloring by the `WriteColor` trait.
For example, to write some green text:

```
use std::io::Write;
use termcolor::{Color, ColorChoice, ColorSpec, StandardStream, WriteColor};
let mut stdout = StandardStream::stdout(ColorChoice::Always);
stdout.set_color(ColorSpec::new().set_fg(Some(Color::Green)))?;
writeln!(&mut stdout, "green text!")?;
```
Note that any text written to the terminal now will be colored
green when using ANSI escape sequences, even if it is written via
stderr, and even if stderr had previously been set to `Color::Red`.
Users will need to manage any color changes themselves by calling
[ WriteColor::set_color](https://docs.rs/trait.WriteColor.html#tymethod.set_color), and this
may include calling

[before the program exits to a shell.](https://docs.rs/trait.WriteColor.html#tymethod.reset)

`WriteColor::reset`[§](https://docs.rs#example-using-bufferwriter)Example: using `BufferWriter`

A `BufferWriter` can create buffers and write buffers to stdout or stderr. It
does *not* implement `io::Write` or `WriteColor` itself. Instead, `Buffer`
implements `io::Write` and `io::WriteColor`.

This example shows how to print some green text to stderr.

```
use std::io::Write;
use termcolor::{BufferWriter, Color, ColorChoice, ColorSpec, WriteColor};
let mut bufwtr = BufferWriter::stderr(ColorChoice::Always);
let mut buffer = bufwtr.buffer();
buffer.set_color(ColorSpec::new().set_fg(Some(Color::Green)))?;
writeln!(&mut buffer, "green text!")?;
bufwtr.print(&buffer)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#detecting-presence-of-a-terminal)Detecting presence of a terminal

In many scenarios when using color, one often wants to enable colors
automatically when writing to a terminal and disable colors automatically when
writing to anything else. The typical way to achieve this in Unix environments
is via libc’s
[ isatty](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/isatty.3.html)
function.
Unfortunately, this notoriously does not work well in Windows environments. To
work around that, the recommended solution is to use the standard library’s

[trait. It goes out of its way to get it as right as possible in Windows environments.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.IsTerminal.html)

`IsTerminal`For example, in a command line application that exposes a `--color` flag,
your logic for how to enable colors might look like this:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::io::IsTerminal;
use termcolor::{ColorChoice, StandardStream};
let preference = argv.get_flag("color").unwrap_or("auto");
let mut choice = preference.parse::<ColorChoice>()?;
if choice == ColorChoice::Auto && !std::io::stdin().is_terminal() {
    choice = ColorChoice::Never;
}
let stdout = StandardStream::stdout(choice);
// ... write to stdout
```
Currently, `termcolor` does not provide anything to do this for you.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ansi](https://docs.rs/struct.Ansi.html)
- Satisfies `WriteColor`using standard ANSI escape sequences.
- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)
- Write colored text to memory.
- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.BufferWriter.html)- Writer
- Writes colored buffers to stdout or stderr.
- [Buffered](https://docs.rs/struct.BufferedStandardStream.html)- Standard - Stream
- Like `StandardStream`, but does buffered writing.
- [Color](https://docs.rs/struct.ColorChoiceParseError.html)- Choice - Parse - Error
- An error that occurs when parsing a `ColorChoice`fails.
- [Color](https://docs.rs/struct.ColorSpec.html)- Spec
- A color specification.
- [Hyperlink](https://docs.rs/struct.HyperlinkSpec.html)- Spec
- A hyperlink specification.
- [NoColor](https://docs.rs/struct.NoColor.html)
- Satisfies `WriteColor`but ignores all color options.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseColorError.html)- Color - Error
- An error from parsing an invalid color specification.
- [Standard](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardStream.html)- Stream
- Satisfies `io::Write`and`WriteColor`, and supports optional coloring to either of the standard output streams, stdout and stderr.
- [Standard](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardStreamLock.html)- Stream - Lock
- `StandardStreamLock`is a locked reference to a- `StandardStream`.

# time - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/time/^0.3.7/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

This crate exposes a number of features. These can be enabled or disabled as shown
[in Cargo’s documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html). Features
are *disabled* by default unless otherwise noted.

Reliance on a given feature is always indicated alongside the item definition.

-
`std`(*enabled by default, implicitly enables*)`alloc`This enables a number of features that depend on the standard library.
-
`alloc`(*enabled by default via*)`std`Enables a number of features that require the ability to dynamically allocate memory.
-
`macros`Enables macros that provide compile-time verification of values and intuitive syntax.
-
`formatting`(*implicitly enables*)`std`Enables formatting of most structs.
-
`parsing`Enables parsing of most structs.
-
`local-offset`(*implicitly enables*)`std`This feature enables a number of methods that allow obtaining the system’s UTC offset.
-
`large-dates`By default, only years within the ±9999 range (inclusive) are supported. If you need support for years outside this range, consider enabling this feature; the supported range will be increased to ±999,999. Note that enabling this feature has some costs, as it means forgoing some optimizations. Ambiguities may be introduced when parsing that would not otherwise exist.
-
`serde`Enables `serde`
-
`serde-human-readable`(*implicitly enables*)`serde`,`formatting`, and`parsing`Allows `serde`representations to use a human-readable format. This is determined by the serializer, not the user. If this feature is not enabled or if the serializer requests a non-human-readable format, a format optimized for binary representation will be used.Libraries should never enable this feature, as the decision of what format to use should be up to the user.
-
`rand`(*implicitly enables*)`rand08`,`rand09`, and`rand010`Previously, this would enable support for `rand`0.8. Since the release of`rand`0.9, the feature has been split into`rand08`and`rand09`to allow support for both versions.`rand`0.10 has since been added. For backwards compatibility and simplicity, this feature enables support for*all*series.It is strongly recommended to enable the version you need directly, as enabling `rand`will needlessly pull in all versions.
-
`rand08`,`rand09`,`rand010`Enables `rand`0.8`rand`0.9`rand`0.10
-
`quickcheck`(*implicitly enables*)`alloc`Enables [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/quickcheck)support for all types.
-
`wasm-bindgen`Enables `wasm-bindgen`[JavaScript dates](https://rustwasm.github.io/wasm-bindgen/api/js_sys/struct.Date.html), as well as obtaining the UTC offset from JavaScript.

# simplelog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/simplelog/latest/target-redirect/simplelog/

## Expand description

`simplelog` provides a series of logging facilities, that can be easily combined.

- `SimpleLogger`(very basic logger that logs to stdout)
- `TermLogger`(advanced terminal logger, that splits to stdout/err and has color support) (can be excluded on unsupported platforms)
- `WriteLogger`(logs to a given struct implementing- `Write`, e.g. a file)
- `CombinedLogger`(can be used to form combinations of the above loggers)
- `TestLogger`(specialized logger for tests. Uses print!() / println!() for tests to be able to capture the output)

Only one Logger should be initialized of the start of your program
through the `Logger::init(...)` method. For the actual calling syntax
take a look at the documentation of the specific implementation(s) you wanna use.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Combined](https://docs.rs/struct.CombinedLogger.html)- Logger
- The CombinedLogger struct. Provides a Logger implementation that proxies multiple Loggers as one.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- Configuration for the Loggers
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for the Logger Configurations (`Config`)
- [Simple](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleLogger.html)- Logger
- The SimpleLogger struct. Provides a very basic Logger implementation
- [Term](https://docs.rs/struct.TermLogger.html)- Logger
- The TermLogger struct. Provides a stderr/out based Logger implementation
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteLogger.html)- Logger
- The WriteLogger struct. Provides a Logger implementation for structs implementing `Write`, e.g. File

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)
- The set of available colors for the terminal foreground/background.
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- ColorChoice represents the color preferences of an end user.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.FormatItem.html)- Item
- A complete description of how to format and parse a type.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)
- An enum representing the available verbosity levels of the logger.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)- Filter
- An enum representing the available verbosity level filters of the logger.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the level
- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.TargetPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the thread id/name
- [Terminal](https://docs.rs/enum.TerminalMode.html)- Mode
- Specifies which streams should be used when logging
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/enum.ThreadLogMode.html)- LogMode
- Mode for logging the thread name or id or both.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_redis - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-backplane-redis/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_backplane_redis/

## Expand description

Redis / Valkey [ Backplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/trait.Backplane.html) — the horizontal scale-out seam.

The default [ InMemoryBackplane](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html) only reaches sockets held by the current
process, so with more than one replica an event produced on pod A can’t reach
a socket on pod B.

[closes that gap](https://docs.rs/struct.RedisBackplane.html)

`RedisBackplane`**without changing the trait or any call site**: it keeps a per-pod

[for the local registry + delivery, and adds a Redis pub/sub bus for cross-pod fan-out.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/backplane/struct.InMemoryBackplane.html)

`InMemoryBackplane`Per call:

- `attach`- `detach`- `associate`- **local**— a connection lives on exactly one pod, so only that pod registers it.
- `publish`- `BackplaneEnvelope`- `Target`- *its own*registry and delivers to its sockets — so the same- `publish`call fans out across the whole fleet. The origin pod skips its own echo (it already delivered).

This is the classic pub/sub fan-out (the shape Socket.IO’s Redis adapter uses): no shared connection registry, each pod authoritative for its own sockets.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Redis](https://docs.rs/struct.RedisBackplane.html)- Backplane
- A `Backplane``publish`out across pods over Redis/Valkey pub/sub.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_CHANNEL.html)- CHANNEL
- Default pub/sub channel. Override via `RedisBackplane::connect_on_channel`

# smooth_operator_adapter_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-memory/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_memory/

## Expand description

In-memory [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the conformance / test baseline.

All OLTP slices (conversations, participants, messages, sessions) live in
`HashMap`s behind a single `RwLock`. The checkpoint and knowledge slices
delegate to smooth-operator’s own [ MemoryCheckpointStore](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/checkpoint/struct.MemoryCheckpointStore.html) and

[, which are exactly what the engine expects — so this adapter is a faithful (if non-durable) stand-in for Postgres/DynamoDB.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/knowledge/struct.InMemoryKnowledge.html)

`InMemoryKnowledge`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# smooth_operator_ingestion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-ingestion/1.11.1/smooth_operator_ingestion/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator-ingestion)smooth-operator ingestion

Knowledge **ingestion + connectors** for smooth-operator — the pipeline
that pulls documents from a source, chunks them, embeds them, and stores them
in the [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html)
knowledge slice so they are retrievable. This closes feature gap G1 (knowledge
ingestion + connectors), G2 (document chunking pipeline), and G9 (the
connector mock +

`unit`-vs-`external` test split). See `docs/INGESTION.md`.[§](https://docs.rs#shape)Shape

```
Connector::pull ─▶ Chunker::chunk ─▶ Embedder::embed ─▶ KnowledgeBase::ingest
   RawDocument        Vec<Chunk>        Vec<Vec<f32>>        (StorageAdapter
                                                              knowledge slice)
```
- `Connector`- `RawDocument`- `pull(since)`). Built-ins:- `FileConnector`- `WebConnector`- `MockConnector`
- `Chunker`
- `Embedder`- `smooth_operator::embedding`- `DeterministicEmbedder`
- `ingest`- `(doc id, content hash)`via an- `IngestLedger`

[§](https://docs.rs#wiring-example)Wiring example

```
let connector = FileConnector::new("./docs");
let report = ingest(
    &connector,
    &Chunker::default(),
    &DeterministicEmbedder::new(),
    storage.knowledge(),
    IngestOptions::for_org("org-acme"),
)
.await?;
println!("stored {} chunks", report.chunks_stored);
```

# smooth_operator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/smooth_operator/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator)smooth-operator

The reference core for smooth-operator — the service layer on top of
[ smooth_operator_core](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/index.html) (the agent engine). It defines three things:

- `domain`- `spec/domain/*.json`. Checkpoints re-use the engine’s- `smooth_operator_core::Checkpoint`
- `adapter`- `StorageAdapter`- `docs/STORAGE.md`). Its checkpoint/knowledge accessors return smooth-operator-core’s own traits so the engine plugs straight in.
- `runtime`- `AgentRuntime`- `Agent`- `Workflow`

It also owns two shared retrieval seams both backends/consumers depend on:
[ embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html) (the text→vector

[+ the network-free](https://docs.rs/embedding/trait.Embedder.html)

`Embedder`[, the one home for both the Postgres adapter and the ingestion pipeline) and](https://docs.rs/embedding/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)

`DeterministicEmbedder`[(the optional post-retrieval](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)

`rerank`[stage — feature gap G8).](https://docs.rs/rerank/trait.Reranker.html)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [access_](https://docs.rs/access_control/index.html)- control
- Document-level access control (feature gap G3).
- [adapter](https://docs.rs/adapter/index.html)
- The `StorageAdapter`seam.
- [agent_](https://docs.rs/agent_config/index.html)- config
- Per-agent behavior config (SMOODEV-590 parity in Rust).
- [auth](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)
- Authentication + role-based access control (Phase 12).
- [backplane](https://docs.rs/backplane/index.html)
- Connection backplane: the scale-out + event-delivery seam for the WebSocket server.
- [connector_](https://docs.rs/connector_config/index.html)- config
- Connector configuration storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [curation](https://docs.rs/curation/index.html)
- Document sets, curation boosting, and query-time metadata filters (feature gap, Phase 11 — “Document sets / curation / boosting”).
- [domain](https://docs.rs/domain/index.html)
- Domain model for smooth-operator.
- [embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html)
- Text → vector embedding — the shared seam for dense retrieval.
- [gateway_](https://docs.rs/gateway_key/index.html)- key
- Per-org LLM gateway-key resolution: the seam that lets a multi-tenant
deployment bill/scope each org’s turns to its **own**gateway key while a standalone/local server keeps using the single environment key.
- [otp](https://docs.rs/otp/index.html)
- End-user identity verification (OTP) — the seam that lets a host wire a
one-time-code flow behind a public agent’s `end_user`tool auth, while the reference server stays credential-free.
- [rerank](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)
- Reranking — the optional post-retrieval reorder stage (feature gap G8).
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Minimal `AgentRuntime`that proves smooth-operator consumes smooth-operator.
- [settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html)
- Per-org agent settings storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [telemetry](https://docs.rs/telemetry/index.html)
- OpenTelemetry GenAI instrumentation for the agent turn.
- [tool_](https://docs.rs/tool_provider/index.html)- provider
- Host-contributed tool injection seam.
- [tools](https://docs.rs/tools/index.html)
- Tools the smooth-operator runtime registers on the smooth-operator-core engine.
- [widget_](https://docs.rs/widget_auth/index.html)- auth
- Embeddable-widget auth: an origin allowlist + public-key `authContext`verification for browser-embedded chat widgets (`<smooth-agent-chat>`).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.Checkpoint.html)
- A checkpoint captures the full state of an agent at a point in time.

# stop - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stop-cli/0.0.2/stop/

## Expand description

Process and system monitoring with structured output.

Provides cross-platform system metrics collection with filtering, sorting, and multiple output formats (JSON, CSV, human-readable).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Data types and collection for system snapshots.

- Error types for the stop CLI tool.

- Filter expression parsing and evaluation for process queries.
- [output](https://docs.rs/output/index.html)
- Output formatting: structured (JSON, CSV) and human-readable display.

- Process filtering pipeline: search → filter → sort → truncate.
- [watch](https://docs.rs/watch/index.html)
- Continuous monitoring (watch mode).

- [SetPsm](https://docs.rs/struct.SetPsmStorageVersionV2.html)- Storage - Version - V2
- One-shot migration: writes `pallet_psm`’s on-chain storage version to v2. Required because`RemovePallet<PsmName>`(above in the migration tuple) wipes the pallet’s`:__STORAGE_VERSION__:`key, and`InitializePsm`doesn’t re-seed it. Without this, try-runtime’s post-upgrade check sees in-code = 2, on-chain = 0 and panics.

# masl_formatter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/masl_formatter/1.0.0/masl_formatter/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#masl_formatter)masl_formatter

Canonical source code formatter for `.mdk` files.

Consumes an `masl_ast::Document` and produces formatted MASL source text.
Never modifies semantics. Guarantees idempotency: fmt(fmt(S)) == fmt(S).

See RFC-0019 — Formatter.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [format](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html)
- Format a parsed AST Document back to canonical MASL source text.

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_total.html)- total
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_sane_fees_values.html)- sane_ - fees_ - values
- A helper function for comparing the actual value of a fee constant with its estimated value. The
estimated value can be overestimated (`overestimate_in_percent`), and if the difference to the actual value is below`margin_overestimate_diff_in_percent_for_lowering`, we should lower the actual value.
- [diff_](https://docs.rs/fn.diff_as_percent.html)- as_ - percent
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/fn.ensure_opened_bridge.html)- opened_ - bridge
- Helper function to open the bridge/lane for `source`and`destination`while ensuring all required balances are placed into the SA of the source.
- [mock_](https://docs.rs/fn.mock_open_hrmp_channel.html)- open_ - hrmp_ - channel
- Helper function which emulates opening HRMP channel which is needed for `XcmpQueue`to pass.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_bridge_with_extrinsic.html)- bridge_ - with_ - extrinsic
- Utility for opening bridge with dedicated `pallet_xcm_bridge_hub`’s extrinsic.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_bridge_with_storage.html)- bridge_ - with_ - storage
- Utility for opening bridge directly inserting data to the `pallet_xcm_bridge_hub`’s storage (used only for legacy purposes).
- [test_](https://docs.rs/fn.test_header.html)- header
- Get a header for testing.

# simplelog 0.12.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/simplelog/0.12.2

## A simple and easy-to-use logging facility for Rust's [log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate

`simplelog` does not aim to provide a rich set of features, nor to provide the
best logging solution. It aims to be a maintainable, easy to integrate facility
for small to medium sized projects, that find [env_logger](https://crates.io/crates/env_logger)
to be somewhat lacking in features. In those cases `simplelog` should provide an
easy alternative.

## Concept

`simplelog` provides a series of logging facilities, that can be easily combined.

- `SimpleLogger`(very basic logger that logs to stderr/out, should never fail)
- `TermLogger`(advanced terminal logger, that splits to stderr/out and has color support) (can be excluded on unsupported platforms)
- `WriteLogger`(logs to a given struct implementing- `Write`. e.g. a file)
- `CombinedLogger`(can be used to form combinations of the above loggers)

## Usage

```
 extern crate log;
extern crate simplelog;
use *;
use File;
```
### Results in

```
$ cargo run --example usage
   Compiling simplelog v0.12.2 (file:///home/drakulix/Projects/simplelog)
     Running `target/debug/examples/usage`
[ERROR] Bright red error
```
and my_rust_binary.log

```
11:13:03 [ERROR] usage: Bright red error
11:13:03 [INFO] usage: This only appears in the log file
```
## Getting Started

Just add

```
[dependencies]
simplelog = "^0.12.2"
```
to your `Cargo.toml`

## ANSI color and style support

This crate can internally depend on a [paris](https://github.com/0x20F/paris) crate to provide support for ANSI color and styles.
To use this feature you need to set a *paris* feature, like this:

```
[dependencies]
simplelog = { version = "^0.12.2", features = ["paris"] }
```
in your `Cargo.toml`

After this you can use e.g. the following call:

```
info!;
```
This will automatically generates terminal control sequences for desired styles.

More formatting info: [paris crate documentation](https://github.com/0x20F/paris)

## Contributing

If you wish to contribute your own logger to `simplelog` or advance/extend existing loggers,
feel free to create a pull request. Just don't blindly assume, that your logger will be accepted.
The rational about this library is, that it is simple to use. This mostly comes down to a small
and easy API, but also includes things like the amount of added dependencies. If you feel unsure
about your plans, feel free to create an issue to talk about your ideas.

---

                    simplelog 0.12.2

# simplelog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/simplelog/0.12.2/target-redirect/simplelog/

## Expand description

`simplelog` provides a series of logging facilities, that can be easily combined.

- `SimpleLogger`(very basic logger that logs to stdout)
- `TermLogger`(advanced terminal logger, that splits to stdout/err and has color support) (can be excluded on unsupported platforms)
- `WriteLogger`(logs to a given struct implementing- `Write`, e.g. a file)
- `CombinedLogger`(can be used to form combinations of the above loggers)
- `TestLogger`(specialized logger for tests. Uses print!() / println!() for tests to be able to capture the output)

Only one Logger should be initialized of the start of your program
through the `Logger::init(...)` method. For the actual calling syntax
take a look at the documentation of the specific implementation(s) you wanna use.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Combined](https://docs.rs/struct.CombinedLogger.html)- Logger
- The CombinedLogger struct. Provides a Logger implementation that proxies multiple Loggers as one.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- Configuration for the Loggers
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for the Logger Configurations (`Config`)
- [Simple](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleLogger.html)- Logger
- The SimpleLogger struct. Provides a very basic Logger implementation
- [Term](https://docs.rs/struct.TermLogger.html)- Logger
- The TermLogger struct. Provides a stderr/out based Logger implementation
- [Write](https://docs.rs/struct.WriteLogger.html)- Logger
- The WriteLogger struct. Provides a Logger implementation for structs implementing `Write`, e.g. File

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)
- The set of available colors for the terminal foreground/background.
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- ColorChoice represents the color preferences of an end user.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.FormatItem.html)- Item
- A complete description of how to format and parse a type.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)
- An enum representing the available verbosity levels of the logger.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)- Filter
- An enum representing the available verbosity level filters of the logger.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the level
- [Target](https://docs.rs/enum.TargetPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the thread id/name
- [Terminal](https://docs.rs/enum.TerminalMode.html)- Mode
- Specifies which streams should be used when logging
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/enum.ThreadLogMode.html)- LogMode
- Mode for logging the thread name or id or both.
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/enum.ThreadPadding.html)- Padding
- Padding to be used for logging the thread id/name

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Shared](https://docs.rs/trait.SharedLogger.html)- Logger
- Trait to have a common interface to obtain the Level of Loggers

# CombinedLogger in simplelog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/simplelog/0.12.2/simplelog/struct.CombinedLogger.html

`pub struct CombinedLogger { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The CombinedLogger struct. Provides a Logger implementation that proxies multiple Loggers as one.

The purpose is to allow multiple Loggers to be set globally

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/simplelog/loggers/comblog.rs.html#46-50)#### pub fn [init](https://docs.rs#method.init)(logger: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [SharedLogger](https://docs.rs/trait.SharedLogger.html)>>) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [SetLoggerError](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/struct.SetLoggerError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/simplelog/loggers/comblog.rs.html#46-50)

#### pub fn [init](https://docs.rs#method.init)(logger: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [SharedLogger](https://docs.rs/trait.SharedLogger.html)>>) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [SetLoggerError](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/log/struct.SetLoggerError.html)>

init function. Globally initializes the CombinedLogger as the one and only used log facility.

Takes all used Loggers as a Vector argument. None of those Loggers should already be set globally.

All loggers need to implement `log::Log` and `logger::SharedLogger` and need to provide a way to be
initialized without calling `set_logger`. All loggers of this library provide a `new(..)`` method
for that purpose.
Fails if another logger is already set globally.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let _ = CombinedLogger::init(
            vec![
                TermLogger::new(LevelFilter::Info, Config::default(), TerminalMode::Mixed, ColorChoice::Auto),
                WriteLogger::new(LevelFilter::Info, Config::default(), File::create("my_rust_bin.log").unwrap())
            ]
        );
```
```
7fn main() {
8    CombinedLogger::init(vec![
9        #[cfg(feature = "termcolor")]
10        TermLogger::new(
11            LevelFilter::Warn,
12            Config::default(),
13            TerminalMode::Mixed,
14            ColorChoice::Auto,
15        ),
16        #[cfg(not(feature = "termcolor"))]
17        SimpleLogger::new(LevelFilter::Warn, Config::default()),
18        WriteLogger::new(
19            LevelFilter::Info,
20            Config::default(),
21            File::create("my_rust_binary.log").unwrap(),
22        ),
23    ])
24    .unwrap();
25
26    error!("Bright red error");
27    info!("This only appears in the log file");
28    debug!("This level is currently not enabled for any logger");
29}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/simplelog/loggers/comblog.rs.html#77-89)#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(logger: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [SharedLogger](https://docs.rs/trait.SharedLogger.html)>>) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<[CombinedLogger](https://docs.rs/struct.CombinedLogger.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/simplelog/loggers/comblog.rs.html#77-89)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(logger: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [SharedLogger](https://docs.rs/trait.SharedLogger.html)>>) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<[CombinedLogger](https://docs.rs/struct.CombinedLogger.html)>

allows to create a new logger, that can be independently used, no matter whats globally set.

no macros are provided for this case and you probably
dont want to use this function, but `init()`, if you dont want to build a `CombinedLogger`.

Takes all used loggers as a Vector argument. The log level is automatically determined by the lowest log level used by the given loggers.

All loggers need to implement log::Log.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
let combined_logger = CombinedLogger::new(
            vec![
                TermLogger::new(LevelFilter::Debug, Config::default(), TerminalMode::Mixed, ColorChoice::Auto),
                WriteLogger::new(LevelFilter::Info, Config::default(), File::create("my_rust_bin.log").unwrap())
            ]
        );
```

# Config in simplelog - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/simplelog/0.12.2/simplelog/struct.Config.html

`pub struct Config { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Configuration for the Loggers

All loggers print the message in the following form:
`00:00:00 [LEVEL] crate::module: [lib.rs::100] your_message`
Every space delimited part except the actual message is optional.

Pass this struct to your logger to change when these information shall be logged.

Construct using [ Default](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html#method.default) or using

`ConfigBuilder`## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)
